title: Chemistry IX · 2019 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Part I Chemistry. It contains official comments on candidates' responses to the 2019 SSC-I Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: Most candidates demonstrated commendable conceptual clarity in physical separation techniques like chromatography and writing electron configurations for first-row ions. However, areas requiring pedagogical reinforcement include distinguishing fixed vs sharp melting points in giant lattice structures, applying kinetic molecular theory to microscopic gas effusion, and systematically calculating stoichiometric molar ratios before finding empirical formulas.

questions.questionText: State any FOUR characteristics of an ionic compound.
questions.sloText: Describe the characteristics and physical properties of ionic compounds.
checkingHints: 1 mark for each valid physical or chemical characteristic of ionic compounds (any 4):
- Crystalline structure / 3D ionic lattice.
- High melting and boiling points.
- Electrical conduction in molten or aqueous states.
- Solubility in polar solvents like water and insolubility in non-polar solvents.
- Hard and brittle nature.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates generally showed good familiarity with the properties of ionic compounds. Better responses articulated exact physical properties such as crystalline lattice formation, high melting/boiling points, electrical conductivity in molten/aqueous phases, and solubility in polar solvents. Weaker responses confused the process of ionic bond formation (transfer of electrons) with the characteristics of the resulting compound, or confused high melting points with sharp/fixed melting points.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed the correct characteristics of ionic compounds. Candidates demonstrated clear understanding of physical properties of ionic compounds including their solubility in water, 3-dimensional crystalline structure, high melting and boiling point, electrical conductance in molten or solution state along with chemical characteristics like polarity, presence of ions, and strong electrostatic force of attraction between ions.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses demonstrated poor conceptual knowledge about the characteristics of ionic compounds. Most of these responses described the formation of ionic bond by complete transfer of electrons but failed to figure out the characteristics. Mostly weaker responses could not determine the difference between high melting point and sharp/fixed melting points. Candidates described about conduction of electricity without mentioning the state as molten or solution form.
suggestions: Emphasize the distinction between bonding mechanism (how the bond is created) and physical properties of the bulk substance.
Highlight the requirement of mobile ions for electrical conduction, explicitly identifying aqueous and molten states.
questions.modelAnswer:
Characteristics of Ionic Compounds:
1. Crystalline 3D Lattice: Form rigid crystal lattices consisting of regularly alternating positive and negative ions.
2. High Melting and Boiling Points: Strong omnidirectional electrostatic attractions require large thermal energy to break.
3. Electrical Conductivity: Non-conductive as solids; good electrical conductors when molten or dissolved in water due to mobile ions.
4. Solubility: Soluble in polar solvents (e.g. water) and insoluble in non-polar organic solvents.

questions.questionText:
An analytical chemist uses chromatography to investigate the types of amino acids present in a mixture of amino acids. He represents the mixture as M, and the known amino acids as 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. During experimentation, he ensures that the base line containing spots is placed above the solvent level. After experimentation, he sprays the chromatogram with a solution of ninhydrin.
a. Why is the base line containing spots placed above the solvent level?
b. What is the purpose of spraying ninhydrin solution on chromatogram?
c. Based on his investigation, identify the amino acids which are present in the mixture.
questions.sloText: Explain the principle and technique of paper chromatography including Rf values and locating agents.
checkingHints: Part a: 1 mark for explaining that baseline must be above solvent so spots do not wash/dissolve directly into the solvent.
Part b: 1 mark for identifying ninhydrin as a locating agent to visualize colorless amino acid spots.
Part c: 2 marks for identifying amino acids 1, 3, and 5 from horizontal spot alignment.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates performed well on interpreting the chromatogram. Better responses clearly recognized that elevating the baseline prevents sample dissolution into the solvent reservoir, correctly identified ninhydrin as a locating agent to reveal colorless amino acids, and matched spots to amino acids 1, 3, and 5. Weaker responses stated that elevating baseline was for measuring distance or drying, and lacked knowledge of locating agents.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed clear understanding of the concept of chromatography. Candidates were able to explain the reason for the placement of the base line above the solvent level in part 'a', i.e. to prevent mixing/dissolving of spots with the solvent. In part 'b', candidates correctly mentioned the purpose of ninhydrin spray is to locate/visualise the colorless spots on the chromatogram. Moreover, in part 'c', candidates successfully identified the composition of the mixture as amino acids 1, 3, and 5.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses depicted lack of conceptual understanding regarding chromatography. In part 'a', candidates wrongly stated the reason for the placement of baseline above the solvent level, i.e. for the measurement of spots/for separation of colour dyes/to prevent chromatogram from getting wet. In part 'b', candidates showed lack of knowledge regarding locating agents, claiming ninhydrin separates or evaporates spots. In part 'c', candidates wrongly identified numbers of amino acids or omitted standards.
suggestions: Conduct hands-on chromatography lab sessions with both colored inks and colorless amino acids using ninhydrin locating spray.
Reinforce baseline setup discipline to ensure spots run along the mobile phase front rather than leaching into the solvent reservoir.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. The baseline is placed above the solvent level so the sample spots do not dissolve directly into the solvent reservoir.
b. Ninhydrin acts as a locating agent that reacts with colorless amino acids to produce visible coloured (purple/pink) spots.
c. Mixture M contains amino acids 1, 3, and 5.

questions.questionText:
Write a reason for each of the following periodic trends observed in the periodic table.
a. Electronegativity increases across the period.
b. Shielding effect increases down the group.
c. Atomic radius decreases across the period.
d. Ionisation energy decreases down the group.
questions.sloText: Explain the periodic trends across periods and down groups.
checkingHints: 1 mark each for correct periodic trend reasoning:
a. Increasing effective nuclear charge attracts shared electron pairs more strongly across a period.
b. Addition of extra shells increases intervening core electrons down a group.
c. Greater nuclear charge pulls electrons of the same shell inward across a period.
d. Increased atomic radius and shielding reduce nuclear pull on valence electrons down a group.
questions.overallPerformance: Periodic trend questions elicited sharp contrast between students who understood the underlying physics of nuclear charge and shielding versus those who simply memorized trends. Better responses grounded all four explanations in effective nuclear charge, number of shells, and shielding. Weaker responses merely restated the trends without giving causes.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses depicted the correct reasoning for the given periodic trends. In part 'a', increase in electronegativity across the period was correctly attributed to increase in nuclear charge attracting the bonding pair of electrons more strongly. In part 'b', shielding effect increase down the group was attributed to additional electron shells and inner electrons. In part 'c', decrease in atomic radius across the period was explained by higher nuclear charge pulling the same shell inward. In part 'd', ionisation energy decrease down the group was attributed to increased distance and shielding weakening nuclear hold on valence electrons.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses showed lack of critical thinking and reasoning skills. In most of the weaker responses, candidates merely repeated the prompt without reasoning, or confused trends across periods with trends down groups.
suggestions: Structure periodic trend instruction around the core duel between nuclear charge (Z_eff) and shielding effect (electron shells).
Encourage students to structure trend explanations with three parts: change in nuclear charge, change in shell/shielding, and resulting effect on outer electrons.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Across a period, increasing nuclear charge with constant shielding pulls bonding electrons closer.
b. Down a group, addition of new electron shells increases the number of inner shielding electrons.
c. Across a period, higher positive nuclear charge pulls the valence shell closer inward, reducing atomic radius.
d. Down a group, increased atomic size and electron shielding weaken nuclear attraction for the outermost electron.

questions.questionText:
Write any ONE similarity and TWO differences between the given atoms A and B.
Atom A: p = 17, n = 20
Atom B: p = 17, n = 18
questions.sloText: Define and describe isotopes of an element with examples.
checkingHints: 1 mark for similarity (same protons / atomic number 17 / same element / same electrons).
2 marks for differences (1 mark each for neutron number 20 vs 18, and mass number 37 vs 35).
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates correctly identified atoms A and B as isotopes of chlorine. Better responses explicitly named the identical atomic number (17 protons) as the similarity and quantified the differences in neutron count (20 vs 18) and nucleon/mass number (37 vs 35). Weaker responses stated that both are neutral or confused protons with mass number.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed clarity of concept regarding isotopes. Candidates identified that both atoms are isotopes of chlorine with identical atomic number (17 protons) and electrons, while clearly listing differences in number of neutrons (20 vs 18) and mass number (37 vs 35).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses depicted a lack of recognition of the isotopes of atoms. Most candidates struggled to identify the element or confused subatomic particle identities, writing vague statements like 'both have letters' or confusing electrons with neutrons.
suggestions: Practice isotopic notation A_Z X drills with various elements so students fluidly deduce protons, neutrons, and mass numbers.
Reinforce that chemical identity is governed strictly by proton number Z.
questions.modelAnswer:
Similarity: Both atoms have 17 protons (same atomic number Z = 17), meaning they are isotopes of the same element, chlorine.
Differences:
1. Number of Neutrons: Atom A has 20 neutrons, while Atom B has 18 neutrons.
2. Mass Number: Atom A has a mass number of 37 (17+20), while Atom B has a mass number of 35 (17+18).

questions.questionText:
Consider a closed container with liquid having weak intermolecular forces. This liquid experiences both, vapour pressure and boiling point at constant temperature.
a. Describe the effect of presence of weak intermolecular forces on the vapour pressure of the liquid. (2 Marks)
b. Relate the vapour pressure (described in part a) with the boiling point of the liquid. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Explain the factors affecting vapour pressure and boiling point of liquids.
checkingHints: Part a: 1 mark for mentioning high rate of evaporation / easy escape of molecules; 1 mark for concluding higher vapour pressure.
Part b: 1 mark for stating that higher vapour pressure corresponds to a lower boiling point.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses logically deduced that weak attractions enable liquid molecules to vaporize with minimal kinetic energy, producing high vapour pressure and consequently a low boiling point. Weaker responses asserted that weak forces produce low vapour pressure or failed to connect vapour pressure to boiling point.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses in part 'a' correctly interpreted that weak intermolecular forces allow molecules to easily break away into the vapor phase, generating high vapour pressure. In part 'b', candidates related high vapour pressure to a low boiling point because less heat is needed to equal atmospheric pressure.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses displayed theoretic inadequacy of the whole context. In part 'a', candidates claimed that weak forces mean weak pressure or confused vapour pressure with external atmospheric pressure.
suggestions: Use dynamic particle simulations showing how intermolecular forces govern evaporation rates in closed versus open systems.
Explicitly define boiling point as the temperature at which internal vapour pressure equals external atmospheric pressure.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Weak intermolecular forces allow surface molecules to escape easily into the gas phase, resulting in a high rate of evaporation and high vapour pressure.
b. Because vapour pressure is high, the liquid rapidly reaches atmospheric pressure at a relatively low temperature, resulting in a low boiling point.

questions.questionText:
Give a scientific reason why gold is
a. used in making jewellery. (1 Mark)
b. alloyed with copper when making jewellery. (1 Mark)
c. extensively used in dentistry. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Describe the physical and chemical properties and uses of noble metals.
checkingHints: Part a: 1 mark for chemical inertness / non-corrosive / high lustre / malleable for jewellery.
Part b: 1 mark for increasing hardness and mechanical strength (pure gold is too soft).
Part c: 1 mark for biocompatibility / resistance to corrosion by oral fluids and acids / non-toxic.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates showed good real-world awareness of gold's applications. Better responses cited chemical inertness and unreactive nature for jewellery, alloy hardening for durability, and non-toxicity/corrosion resistance for dental fillings. Weaker responses provided vague aesthetic answers like 'it looks pretty' or 'it is expensive'.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses furnished scientific reasoning. They showed that gold is noble, resistant to corrosion and tarnishing, and malleable for jewellery. They explained copper is added to increase hardness since 24k gold is too soft, and cited biocompatibility and resistance to saliva acids for dentistry.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses indicated awareness of general metal properties but failed to give scientific reasons, stating economic reasons ('gold is rich/costly') rather than chemical inertness and hardness.
suggestions: Connect everyday uses of elements to their position in the reactivity series and standard reduction potentials.
Explain metal alloy structure and why substituting differently sized atoms (copper in gold) prevents lattice slip, increasing hardness.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Gold is noble, chemically unreactive, and resistant to corrosion and tarnishing, while being malleable for crafting.
b. Pure gold is too soft; alloying with copper hardens the metal and increases wear resistance.
c. Gold is chemically inert, non-toxic, and biocompatible, resisting corrosion by saliva and food acids.

questions.questionText:
A compound contains 24% carbon, 12% hydrogen and 64% oxygen by mass. The relative molecular mass of this compound is 50.057 g/mol.
i. Calculate the empirical formula of the given compound. (5 Marks)
ii. Determine its molecular formula. (2 Marks)
(Note: Atomic mass of C = 12 amu, H = 1 amu and O = 16 amu)
questions.sloText: Determine the empirical formula and molecular formula of a compound from percentage composition and molecular mass.
checkingHints: Part i (5 marks): 1 mark for grams per 100g; 2 marks for calculating moles (C=2, H=12, O=4); 1 mark for simplest ratio (1:6:2); 1 mark for empirical formula CH6O2.
Part ii (2 marks): 1 mark for empirical mass 50 and n = 1; 1 mark for molecular formula CH6O2.
questions.overallPerformance: Calculations for empirical and molecular formula were popular among students. Better responses systematically laid out tabular columns for mass, atomic mass, moles, and mole ratios, deriving CH6O2 and n=1. Weaker responses inverted mole calculations (multiplying percentage by atomic mass) or skipped finding moles and divided percentages directly.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses had accurate and systematically written steps: calculating moles of C, H, and O, dividing by the smallest mole value to find the atomic ratio (1:6:2), stating empirical formula CH6O2, calculating empirical mass (50 g/mol), and concluding molecular formula CH6O2 with n=1.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses showed inability to present sequential data. Candidates used percentages directly as atomic ratios rather than finding moles, or divided percentage by molecular mass of the entire compound.
suggestions: Drill the standard 4-step algorithm for empirical formulas: % -> grams -> moles -> simplest mole ratio.
Insist that students explicitly calculate empirical formula mass before solving for molecular factor n.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Moles of C = 24/12 = 2; Moles of H = 12/1 = 12; Moles of O = 64/16 = 4.
Dividing by smallest (2): C = 1, H = 6, O = 2.
Empirical formula = CH6O2.
ii. Empirical mass = 12 + 6(1) + 2(16) = 50 g/mol.
n = 50.057 / 50 ≈ 1.
Molecular formula = CH6O2.

questions.questionText:
Given below are four elements: Chlorine (35_17 Cl), Magnesium (24_12 Mg), Oxygen (16_8 O), Potassium (39_19 K).
i. Identify TWO elements from the given table which, when form ions, show the same electronic arrangement as a neon (20_10 Ne) atom. (2 Marks)
ii. Illustrate the formation of an ionic compound using the elements identified in part i with the help of dot and cross structure of the compound. (5 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the formation of ionic bonds using dot and cross structures for simple binary compounds.
checkingHints: Part i (2 marks): 1 mark for Magnesium (Mg2+ has 10 e-); 1 mark for Oxygen (O2- has 10 e-).

Part ii (5 marks): 1 mark for neutral atom configurations; 1 mark for showing transfer of 2 electrons; 1 mark for Mg2+ cation; 1 mark for O2- anion with octet of dots and crosses; 1 mark for MgO formula.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses identified Magnesium and Oxygen as forming isoelectronic ions with neon (10 electrons) and drew meticulous dot and cross diagrams showing the complete transfer of two valence electrons from Mg to O, producing [Mg]2+ and [:Ö:]2-. Weaker responses picked Chlorine and Potassium (which acquire Argon configuration, 18 electrons) or drew covalent shared pairs for MgO.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses successfully identified Magnesium and Oxygen as acquiring neon's 2,8 electronic configuration. They illustrated the transfer of two electrons from Mg to O with dot and cross diagrams and clearly showed the resulting ionic lattice ions [Mg]2+ and [O]2-.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to identify the correct atoms in part 'i', picking chlorine or potassium. In part 'ii', candidates drew covalent bonds with overlapping circles rather than ionic electron transfer and bracketed charges.
suggestions: Practice isoelectronic species drills comparing ions of Period 2 and Period 3 with Neon and Argon noble gas octets.
Differentiate sharply between electron sharing (covalent overlapping circles) and complete electron transfer (ionic brackets with net charge).
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Magnesium (Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-) and Oxygen (O + 2e- -> O2-) both achieve Neon's 10-electron configuration (2, 8).
ii. Mg (2, 8, 2) transfers 2 valence electrons to O (2, 6) forming [Mg]2+ and [ :Ö: ]2-, producing ionic magnesium oxide (MgO).

questions.questionText:
i. Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases. (6 Marks)
ii. What happens to the particles during effusion in gases? (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in three states of matter and explain effusion in gases.
checkingHints: Part i (6 marks): 1 mark for arrangement and 1 mark for movement in each of solid, liquid, and gas phases.
Part ii (1 mark): 1 mark for explaining gas particles escaping through a tiny pinhole into lower pressure without collisions.
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates generally scored well on describing states of matter. Better responses clearly distinguished the vibrational movement of closely packed solid particles, sliding movement of liquid particles, and high-speed random translational movement of widely separated gas particles. For effusion, better responses described particles escaping one by one through a tiny pinhole.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses systematically described particle arrangement and motion across all three states using kinetic molecular theory terminology. In part 'ii', candidates accurately described effusion as gas particles escaping through a tiny microscopic aperture or pinhole.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to explain movement, describing macro shapes instead ('liquids take the shape of container'). In part 'ii', candidates confused effusion with general diffusion or evaporation.
suggestions: Require students to use microscopic particle language (vibrational, translational, intermolecular spacing) rather than macroscopic descriptions.
Clearly distinguish diffusion (spreading through another gas) from effusion (escaping through a pinhole into a vacuum/lower pressure).
questions.currentTopic: States of Matter & Kinetic Molecular Theory
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Solids: tightly packed in regular lattice, vibrate in fixed positions. Liquids: closely packed in random arrangement, slide past each other. Gases: far apart with large spaces, move rapidly and randomly in all directions.
ii. During effusion, gas particles escape one by one through a tiny pinhole into an area of lower pressure due to their rapid random motion.

questions.questionText:
The given diagram shows different conditions to investigate rusting of iron.
Test Tube I: Nail in ordinary water open to air
Test Tube II: Nail with anhydrous calcium chloride (drying agent) sealed with stopper
Test Tube III: Nail in boiled water (no dissolved air) covered with layer of oil and sealed with stopper
Test Tube IV: Nail in salt water open to air
i. In which of the given test tubes, I to IV, will the iron nail rust? Explain why the iron nail rusts in the identified test tube(s) and not in others. (6 Marks)
ii. Why is the process of rusting a redox reaction? (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Explain the conditions necessary for rusting of iron and justify corrosion as an electrochemical redox process.
checkingHints: Part i (6 marks): 1 mark for identifying Test Tubes I and IV; 1 mark for explaining Tube I (water + O2); 1 mark for Tube IV (water + O2 + electrolyte accelerating rust); 1 mark for Tube II (no water, dry air); 1 mark for Tube III (no oxygen, boiled water + oil); 1 mark for concluding both water and oxygen are essential.
Part ii (1 mark): 1 mark for stating iron is oxidised (loses electrons) and oxygen is reduced (gains electrons).
questions.overallPerformance: Rusting of iron in controlled test tubes is a classic experimental benchmark. Better responses identified test tubes I and IV, explaining how anhydrous CaCl2 removes moisture in II, boiled water and oil exclude oxygen in III, and salt in IV accelerates electrochemical conduction. Better responses also wrote oxidation and reduction equations to justify redox.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses efficiently identified test tubes I and IV, providing rigorous scientific rationales for each tube. Candidates highlighted salt as an electrolyte that speeds up electron transfer in tube IV. In part 'ii', candidates clearly explained that Fe undergoes oxidation (losing electrons) while O2 undergoes reduction (gaining electrons).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses identified only tube I, missing tube IV or claiming salt prevents rust. In part 'ii', candidates defined redox generally without connecting it to iron losing electrons and oxygen gaining electrons.
suggestions: Set up the 4-tube rusting experiment in the classroom over 1-2 weeks so students directly observe the accelerated rusting in salt water and total prevention in dry/deoxygenated tubes.
Explicitly write the half-reactions for corrosion to demonstrate electron transfer.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Rusting occurs in Test Tubes I and IV (fastest in IV). Tube I has both water and oxygen. Tube IV has water, oxygen, and salt electrolyte which speeds up rusting. Tube II has no water (CaCl2 drying agent). Tube III has no oxygen (boiled water and oil barrier).
ii. Rusting is redox because metallic iron is oxidised (Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-) while dissolved oxygen is reduced (O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-).
